orders.description: Appeal from the September 26, 2019 order granting defendants summary judgment, continued by the substituted estate administrator.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Christopher Yerry allegedly slipped on a puddle of liquid inside defendants' supermarket. Employees' incomplete remedial measures were alleged to have worsened the condition.

legal_issues.finding: Defendants did not establish adequate and timely remedial action following actual notice; the warning/remediation obligation remained relevant despite the obviousness defense.
Defendants' evidence raised a factual issue whether employees exacerbated the condition through incomplete remedial measures, not a conclusive finding of creation or worsening.
The court addressed measures taken after actual notice and found defendants' initial showing insufficient to negate a causally relevant failure to remediate within reasonable time.
Constructive notice is part of the stated initial-burden standard; the application focuses on actual notice and remediation rather than a separate constructive-notice finding.
Defendants failed to establish that the liquid condition was both open and obvious and not inherently dangerous.
The unsigned but certified employee and plaintiff deposition transcripts were properly considered. That evidentiary ruling accompanied substantive negligence review.

evidence_discussed.description: Yerry's deposition testimony was submitted; its unsigned but certified transcripts were properly considered.
Defendants' employee deposition transcript was unsigned but certified and properly considered.

quality.notes: Private retail control is supported by defendants' supermarket and employees' remediation. Liquid composition is unspecified; other hazard records liquid without inferring water, grease or another substance. The injured person is Christopher, not substituted administrator Judith. His later death is not attributed to the fall. Plaintiff's customer/visitor status and accident date are unstated. Transcript admissibility does not make this appeal procedural-only.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is reversed, on the law, with costs, and the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint is denied.

Christopher Yerry (hereinafter Yerry) commenced this action against the defendants to recover damages for personal injuries he allegedly sustained when he slipped and fell on a puddle of liquid inside the defendants' supermarket.
The order granted the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

Here, viewing the evidence in the light most favorable to Yerry as the nonmovant, the defendants failed to establish, prima facie, that the accident was not the result of the defendants' failure to take appropriate remedial measures within a reasonable period of time after acquiring actual notice of a hazardous condition

The evidence submitted by the defendants in support of their motion demonstrated the existence of a triable issue of fact as to whether the defendants' employees made the condition "more hazardous [*2] by incomplete remedial measures"

Moreover, the evidence submitted by the defendants, including, inter alia, Yerry's deposition testimony, failed to establish, prima facie, that the subject condition was open and obvious and not inherently dangerous
Contrary to Yerry's contention, in deciding the motion, the Supreme Court properly considered the unsigned but certified transcript of the deposition of the defendants' employee
as well as the unsigned but certified transcripts of the plaintiff's deposition

Accordingly, since the defendants failed to meet their prima facie burden, the Supreme Court should have denied their motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint without regard to the sufficiency of Yerry's opposition papers

"A defendant who moves for summary judgment in a slip-and-fall case has the initial burden of making a prima facie showing that it neither created the hazardous condition nor had actual or constructive notice of its existence for a sufficient length of time to discover and remedy it"

orders.description: Defendants' limited appeal from the April 27, 2015 order denying the complaint-dismissal portion of their motion.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied the part of defendants' motion seeking summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff slipped on ice beneath snow in COR's parking lot, which Lawn Tech maintained under a snow-removal contract. Plaintiff proposed that piles from earlier plowing had melted and refrozen at the fall location.

legal_issues.finding: An ongoing storm suspended defendants' snow/ice removal duty until a reasonable time after cessation; incomplete removal alone did not establish negligence.
The plowing-pile melt/refreeze theory was speculative; failing to remove all snow and ice during the storm did not itself constitute creation.
Plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue concerning actual notice of a preexisting slippery condition; this was not a conclusive finding about all possible notice.
Plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue concerning constructive notice of a preexisting condition; competent proof of the supposed prior snow pile was absent.
Defendants established an ongoing storm. Plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of a preexisting condition and notice that would defeat the defense.
No competent evidence linked an earlier pile near the fall location to melting/refreezing that caused this fall; the proposed causal chain was speculative.
The weather-site printouts on which plaintiff relied were inadmissible; the court also substantively assessed the snow-pile theory and storm defense.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiff relied on website weather-data printouts to infer prior snow piles; the court expressly treated those printouts as inadmissible.
The snow-removal contract set out general practices; it did not establish a particular pile near the fall site.

quality.notes: The entire appealed complaint-dismissal branch was reversed and the complaint dismissed. 'Granted in part' refers to a limited motion/appeal and does not establish a mixed appellate disposition. Ownership of the lot and the contractor's role are explicit; a contract-specific third-party duty exception is not separately analyzed. The court assumed possible entitlement to the melt/refreeze theory arguendo, without resolving that threshold. Accident date, plaintiff's role and associated premises use are unstated.

evidence.quote: It is hereby ordered that the order insofar as appealed from is unanimously reversed on the law without costs, the motion is granted in part and the complaint is dismissed.

Memorandum: Plaintiff commenced this action seeking damages for injuries she sustained when she slipped and fell on ice underneath snow in a parking lot owned by defendant COR Development Company, LLC and maintained pursuant to a snow removal contract by defendant Lawn Tech, Inc.
The order, insofar as appealed from, denied that part of the motion of defendants for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

It is undisputed that defendants met their initial burden on the motion “by establishing that a storm was in progress at the time of the accident and, thus, that they had no duty to remove the snow and ice until a reasonable time ha[d] elapsed after cessation of the storm”

In opposition, plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact “ ‘whether the accident was caused by a slippery condition at the location where [she] fell that existed prior to the storm, as opposed to precipitation from the storm in progress, and that the defendant [s] had actual or constructive notice of the preexisting condition’ ”

Even assuming, arguendo, that plaintiff was entitled to rely upon the theory that the icy condition formed prior to the storm upon the melting and refreezing of snow piles created by defendants’ plowing *1570 practices
we conclude that plaintiff’s assertion is based on mere speculation and thus is insufficient to raise an issue of fact
Indeed, in surmising that there must have been snow piles throughout the parking lot from prior accumulations, plaintiff relied upon inadmissible printouts from a weather data website
as well as defendants’ general practices regarding snow removal as set forth in their contract

The record is devoid of competent evidence that any such snow piles existed or, more specifically, that a pile of snow was located near the area of the parking lot where plaintiff fell that had melted and had then refrozen prior to the storm, resulting in the icy condition that caused plaintiff’s accident
we note that it is well settled that “ ‘[t]he mere failure to remove all snow and ice from a . . . parking lot does not constitute negligence’ and does not constitute creation of a hazard”
Defendants, as limited by their brief on appeal, contend that Supreme Court erred in denying their motion insofar as they sought summary judgment dismissing the complaint. We agree.

orders.description: Plaintiff's appeal from the June 17, 2019 order granting defendant summary judgment.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff testified that she slipped on a slippery stain under the table where she was dining in defendant's restaurant in February 2017. The manager described general cleaning and inspection policies but no specific pre-fall inspection.

legal_issues.finding: The court placed the initial noncreation burden on defendant, not plaintiff; the opinion's application does not separately resolve creation.
Actual notice is included in the initial-burden rule, but the application resolves constructive-notice sufficiency without a separate actual-notice finding.
General cleaning/inspection policies did not establish when the area was last inspected or cleaned; defendant failed to show lack of constructive notice.
Defendant failed to establish inability to identify the cause; plaintiff's testimony identified a slippery stain underneath her dining table.
The court corrected allocation of the initial summary-judgment burden to defendant; substantive causation and notice showings were insufficient.

evidence_discussed.description: Defendant submitted plaintiff's deposition identifying a slippery stain under her dining table.
The managing partner's deposition addressed only general cleaning/inspection policies, not a specific pre-fall inspection.

quality.notes: Private restaurant control is supported by defendant's restaurant and its managing partner's policies; title ownership is not inferred. Customer is supported by actual dining testimony. Only February 2017 is stated; accident_date is null. Other hazard records a slippery stain of unknown composition, without assuming grease or water. No specific cleaning/inspection records are identified, so evidence is coded as testimony rather than records.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is reversed, on the law, with costs, and the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint is denied.

In June 2017, the plaintiff commenced this action against the defendant to recover damages for personal injuries that she alleged she sustained in February of that year, when she slipped and fell inside the defendant's restaurant in Poughkeepsie.
The order granted the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
Here, the defendant failed to establish, prima facie, that the plaintiff did not know what had caused her to fall

In support of its motion, the defendant submitted, inter alia, the [*2] transcript of the deposition testimony of the plaintiff, who testified that she slipped and fell due to a slippery stain on the floor underneath the table where she was dining.
The defendant also failed to show, prima facie, that it did not have constructive notice of the condition that the plaintiff alleged caused her to fall.

Although the defendant submitted the transcript of the deposition testimony of the individual who was the managing partner of the restaurant at the time of the accident, the manager testified only as to the restaurant's general cleaning and inspection policy and not about any inspections that may have occurred prior to the plaintiff's fall.

Accordingly, since the defendant failed to establish its prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law, the Supreme Court should have denied the defendant's motion without regard to the sufficiency of the plaintiff's opposition papers

Contrary to the court's determination, in a slip-and-fall case, the defendant moving for summary judgment, not the plaintiff, "has the burden of making a prima facie showing that it neither (1) affirmatively created the hazardous condition nor (2) had actual or constructive notice of the condition and a reasonable time to correct or warn about its existence"

"To meet its initial burden on the issue of lack of constructive notice, the defendant must offer some evidence as to when the area in question was last cleaned or inspected relative to the time when the plaintiff fell"

orders.description: Plaintiff's appeal from the December 12, 2014 order granting defendant summary judgment.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff, who lived in the building, allegedly slipped on its exterior staircase during an evening with mist. His deposition did not identify a cause; his later affidavit attributed the fall to rain-wet stairs.

legal_issues.finding: Defendant established plaintiff's inability to identify a cause without speculation through his deposition; the contradictory later rain account raised only a feigned issue.
Plaintiff submitted no expert testimony demonstrating dangerousness of the staircase when wet; the court treated mere rain wetness as insufficient.
The court rejected the contradictory opposing affidavit as a feigned factual issue, alongside substantive cause/dangerous-condition analysis.
Mere rain wetness on the walking surface did not raise a triable issue, particularly without expert proof of dangerousness when wet.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiff's deposition and opposing affidavit differed on knowledge of rain and the cause of the fall; the court rejected the later account as feigned.
Expert testimony demonstrating staircase dangerousness when wet was not submitted; this is an absence, not an expert opinion the annotator reviewed.

quality.notes: The staircase is external and outside a building attributed to defendant. The supplied opinion does not expressly establish ownership/control or private status of that accident staircase; the condominium name alone is not used to resolve the boundary. Retain source evidence for human application of the current rule. Residential use is supported by plaintiff living there, but tenancy/ownership is not specified, so injured_role other means resident. Water is the later contested rain account, not an accepted cause. No actual rain record, expert report or accident date is supplied.

evidence.quote: Order, Supreme Court, New York County (Joan A. Madden, J.), entered December 12, 2014, which granted defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint, unanimously affirmed, without costs.

Plaintiff allegedly slipped and fell on an external staircase outside of defendant's building, where he lived. Plaintiff testified that the staircase was slippery, but he did not know what caused him to fall. He also testified that he could not remember if it had rained that day, but it was misting in the evening, when he fell.

After defendant moved for summary judgment, plaintiff claimed in his affidavit in opposition that the stairs were wet and slippery from rain earlier in the day, and that he slipped and fell as he descended the stairs.
Defendant made a prima facie showing of its entitlement to summary judgment by pointing to plaintiff's deposition testimony that he did not know what caused him to fall
Plaintiff's affidavit, which contradicted his deposition testimony, created only a feigned issue of fact, and was insufficient to defeat defendant's motion

Moreover, mere wetness on a walking surface due to rain is insufficient to raise a triable issue of fact, especially since plaintiff failed to submit any expert testimony showing that the staircase was dangerous when wet

orders.description: Yankees' appeal from the order entered on or about August 12, 2010 denying dismissal of the complaint and cross-claims against it.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied the Yankees' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint and all cross-claims against it.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on ice at the edge of an open transformer vault where Consolidated Edison was working. Consolidated Edison owned the vault; the opinion also addresses snow-removal efforts by the Yankees.

legal_issues.finding: The court assigned maintenance responsibility for the vault area to its owner Consolidated Edison and dismissed the claims against the Yankees.
No evidence raised a triable issue that the Yankees' snow-removal efforts caused, created or exacerbated the hazardous condition.

quality.notes: The actual accident structure, not merely adjoining premises, is expressly owned by Consolidated Edison; private status rests on this ownership evidence. Other premises/location denotes a transformer-vault edge without inventing a sidewalk, street, construction-site or parking setting. Defendant_roles owner refers to Consolidated Edison; other refers to the Yankees' described snow-removal activity, with no contract inferred. Complaint and cross-claims against the sole appellant are dismissed together, so this is substantive negligence review and a full reversal of the appealed order, not third-party-only or mixed. The short opinion identifies no specific evidence types, accident date or plaintiff's role.

evidence.quote: Order, Supreme Court, Bronx County (Mary Brigantti-Hughes, J.), entered on or about August 12, 2010, which denied the motion of defendant New York Yankees Partnership (Yankees) for summary judgment dismissing the complaint and all cross claims as against it, unanimously reversed, on the law, without costs, and the motion granted.

Dismissal of the complaint and all cross claims as against the Yankees is appropriate in this action where plaintiff was injured when he allegedly slipped and fell on an icy condition on the *614 edge of an open transformer vault where Consolidated Edison was working.
The vault was owned by defendant Consolidated Edison, which had a duty to maintain such area.
Furthermore, no evidence was presented which raised a triable issue of fact concerning whether the snow removal efforts by the Yankees caused or created the hazardous condition or exacerbated it
The Clerk is directed to enter judgment accordingly.
